keyVerseText: And when he was come to the other side into the country of the Gergesenes, there met him two possessed with devils, coming out of the tombs, exceeding fierce, so that no man might pass by that way.
rootMeaning: The Greek verb ὑπαντάω (hypantáō) is formed from the preposition ὑπό (hypó), meaning 'under' or 'among,' combined with a derivative of ἀντί (anti), which conveys opposition or encounter. Literally, it carries the sense of going 'under' or 'toward' someone to meet them face-to-face, suggesting a purposeful movement to encounter or fall in with another. This root meaning enriches the English gloss 'to meet' by emphasizing an intentional approach or confrontation rather than a casual or incidental meeting.
usageInScripture: In Scripture, ὑπαντάω appears five times and is most commonly translated as 'there met' or simply 'met,' with one occurrence rendered 'went and met.' This consistency in translation highlights the verb's primary sense of meeting someone, whether as a friend or in conflict, as seen in contexts ranging from personal encounters to battle. The term's usage suggests both physical approach and relational engagement, indicating an active meeting rather than a passive or accidental one.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ὑπαντάω deepens our grasp of biblical narratives where meeting others is not incidental but purposeful and often charged with significance. It portrays encounters as intentional acts that can lead to transformation, confrontation, or revelation—key themes in the Christian faith. This verb reminds believers that God meets His people actively and personally, going out to encounter them in their circumstances. It also invites reflection on the believer's call to go and meet others with the gospel, embodying Christ's proactive love and engagement with a fallen world.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 8:28, the phrase 'there met him two possessed with devils' uses ὑπαντάω to describe a striking, intentional encounter as Jesus arrives in the country of the Gergesenes. The word underscores that this meeting was not accidental but a significant confrontation between Jesus and these tormented men. It highlights the active nature of Jesus' ministry—He goes to meet those in bondage, initiating a powerful encounter that brings deliverance and restoration.
